big_idea: The MODE is the value that appears MOST often. Some data sets have NO mode or MORE THAN ONE.
learning_intention: We are learning to find the mode.
student_learning_goal: I can find the mode of a data set.
success_criteria: I can FIND the most-common value.
I can recognize when there's NO mode.
I can recognize when there's MORE THAN ONE mode.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Tally: This bar graph shows pets. DOG bar is HIGHEST. Dog is the MODE — most common! Dot opens: 'Most counts wins — that's the MODE!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot and Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday bar graphs. Today MODE.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write MODE on chart. 'Mode = the value that appears MOST OFTEN.'

Demo. Show a bar graph: dogs 8, cats 5, fish 2. 'Dogs is highest. Mode = DOGS.'

More examples:
- Sport: hockey 7, soccer 5, baseball 3. Mode = HOCKEY.
- Snack: apple 4, cookie 4, sandwich 3. TWO modes — apple AND cookie. (BIMODAL.)
- Colour: red 3, blue 3, green 3. NO mode (all same — no single most-common).

'Tally says — mode = MOST. If two are tied for most = TWO modes. If all are tied = NO mode.'

'Today we find modes in tables, pictographs, bar graphs.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: find the mode in 4 different displays.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Which is most? That's the mode.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. A: Bar Graph mode. B: Tally Mode. C: Pictograph Mode.
Stretch at Station C: find a 'NO MODE' or 'TWO MODES' example.

STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share how they found the mode on the same graph — Pair A 'I read all heights, picked tallest'; Pair B 'I scanned for the longest bar, then read the label.' Class debates which is more reliable when bars are close in height. Cite Konold & Higgins (2003) — informal-to-formal data reasoning.
steps.teacher_prompt: Dot: 'Different paths to the mode. Both work — but COUNTING beats EYEBALLING when bars are close.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Single mode only.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'The mode is ___ because it appears ___ times.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children stand in lines by answer; tallest line = mode.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: finds mode in bar graph; finds mode in tally; recognizes no-mode and bimodal.

discussion_prompts: Why do detectives care about mode?
consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's mode refrain — class chants: 'Most counts wins — that's the MODE!' Each child reads one graph's mode aloud with the sentence frame.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says 'highest bar' for everything, including ties — repairing the mode-mistake trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On 'find the mode', the trap is identifying the largest VISUAL element rather than the most-frequent CATEGORY. Konold & Higgins (2003, 'Reasoning About Data') and Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001) Level 1 (read the data) place this confusion as central to early data literacy. Without it, Lesson 5's capstone analysis cannot ground.

Yesterday Lesson 3 read bar heights as counts. Today we name the mode — the category with the highest count. Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C. Pictograph: red 4, blue 4, green 3. Child says 'red is the mode'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You picked red. But Tally asks — count blue too. What's blue's count?'

Child: '4'. 'And red?' '4'. 'TIED! That's BIMODAL — TWO modes.'

Guide. 'Red AND Blue both = 4. Both are modes.'

More: '3-3-3 = no mode (all tied).'

Generalise. 'Tally says — count carefully. Tied for highest = TWO modes. All tied = NO mode.'

If still confused: provide pre-built examples. '3 cases: single mode, bimodal, no mode.'

Long-term recovery: every mode check counts all values.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Predicts mode from data before checking.
common_misconceptions: Mode = tallest bar always. (Repair: check ties.)
Mode = unique answer. (Repair: can be 0, 1, or more modes.)
Mode = average. (Repair: mode = most common; not the same as average.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names tallest bar visually but says wrong category: drill 'point and read' — finger on bar, then finger on x-axis label; SAY both.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can identify mode but can't articulate it: force the sentence frame 'The MODE is ___ because it has the MOST ___.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child treats ties incorrectly: drill 'two categories tied = TWO modes (or no single mode)'; child labels tied categories explicitly.

parts_outline.task: Find the mode in 4 displays (bar, pictograph, tally, line plot).
Identify 2 special cases: NO mode and TWO modes.
Make your own data set with a clear mode.
